'''Janet Turk Wittes''' is an American [[Biostatistics|biostatistician]] and entrepreneur, known for her work on statistical issues in [[clinical trial]]s.{{r|AmStatNews2020}} She is the former chief of statistics at the National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute. One of her three children is [[Benjamin Wittes]], legal and national security journalist.{{r|Lawfare}}
==Education==
Wittes is the daughter of a chemist and a psychologist. She began her studies at [[Radcliffe College]] in the [[biochemistry]] program, choosing it over chemistry because of its added opportunities for mentorship. Her faculty mentor, [[John Tileston Edsall]], noting her preference for [[inference]] over experiment, guided her to aim for a career in statistics. Towards this goal, Wittes switched her major to mathematics,{{r|chance}} graduating in 1964.{{r|norwood}}

Wittes stayed at [[Harvard University]] for her graduate studies in statistics. At Harvard, she was supported by a fellowship from the [[United States Public Health Service]] (chosen because its application form was short) and because of this ended up working in [[biostatistics]].{{r|chance}} Wittes completed her Ph.D. in 1970;{{r|norwood}} her [[doctoral advisor]] was Theodore Colton.{{r|chance}}

==Career==
While her husband, physician [[Robert E. Wittes]],{{r|hub}} served a term in the [[United States Public Health Service Commissioned Corps]], Wittes did part-time postdoctoral research with [[Jerome Cornfield]] at the [[National Cancer Institute]]. After an additional two years as a part-time instructor of [[epidemiology]] at [[Columbia University]],{{r|chance}} she became a regular-rank faculty member in the mathematics department at [[Hunter College]] in 1974 and remained there until 1982.{{r|chance|norwood}}

In 1983 Wittes moved to the [[National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute]] as chief of the Biostatistics Research Branch, and remained there until 1988,{{r|norwood}} when she left because of a change of employment by her husband,{{r|chance}} and became a biostatistician for the [[Department of Veterans Affairs]] in Connecticut from 1989 to 1990.{{r|norwood}} 

Upon the family's return to Washington in 1990, and unable to find a suitable government position, Wittes founded a consulting firm, Statistics Collaborative.{{r|chance}} She ran the company for almost 30 years, focusing on providing specialized biostatistical consulting services to developers of new drugs and biologics, with a focus is on late-stage clinical trials. She worked on trial design, reporting for Data Monitoring Committees, data analysis, and consultation for FDA presentations.{{r|WCG_PR}} In 2020, Wittes sold the company, Statistics Collaborative, to WCG Clinical, Inc.{{r|WCG_PR|Smith20201214}}

==Research and Publication==
Wittes' research focuses on the design of [[clinical trial]]s, and she has also published on [[mark and recapture]] methods.{{r|norwood}}
With Michael A. Proschan and K. K. Gordon Lan, she is an author of the book ''Statistical Monitoring of Clinical Trials: A Unified Approach'' (Springer, 2006, {{ISBN|978-0-387-44970-8}}).{{r|smct}}
 
Wittes was president of the Society for Clinical Trials for 2001. She was editor-in-chief of the society's journal ''Controlled Clinical Trials'' from 1994 to 1998.{{r|norwood}}

==Recognition==
Wittes was elected as a [[Fellow of the American Statistical Association]] in 1989. She is also a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] and of the Society for Clinical Trials, and an elected member of the [[International Statistical Institute]]{{r|chance}}

Wittes was the winner of the 2006 Janet L. Norwood Award For Outstanding Achievement By A Woman In The Statistical Sciences.{{r|norwood}}
In 2015 the [[American Statistical Association]] gave her their W. J. Dixon Award for Excellence in Statistical Consulting "for exceptional contributions to advancing the science and art of statistical consulting and collaboration; for developing innovative, widely used, statistical methodology; for major worldwide accomplishments, especially in the area of clinical trials, including performing creative, easily interpretable interim analyses and serving on numerous data and safety monitoring boards; for extraordinary leadership as president of Statistics Collaborative; and for being a true beacon for integrity."{{r|dixon}}
